lessons.title: Lesson 1: Using AI safely for money questions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant a money question safely, with no private details.
This lesson builds toward: When you have a money question, you will ask an AI assistant the question using rounded numbers and no private details, sharing no account, card or identity numbers.
An AI assistant can explain money words, build a budget table, compare options you give it, and turn a messy list of bills into a plan. It is a fast, patient helper.
It is not a financial advisor. It does not know your full situation, it can be wrong about rules and numbers, and it can be out of date. Use it to understand and organize; check decisions with an official source or a qualified counselor.
Never type your Social Security number, your DD-214 or VA file numbers, bank or card numbers, account logins or passwords into an AI. Use rounded numbers instead: "rent about $1,200" is all it needs.
Step by step:
- Decide what you want: an explanation, a table or a plan.
- Use rounded numbers, no account details.
- Ask the question.
- Mark any rule, rate or deadline to check with an official source.
Words to know:
- Budget: a plan for how your money comes in and goes out each month.
- Rounded number: a close, simple number like $1,200 instead of an exact figure tied to an account.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "Explain the difference between a need and a want in a monthly budget, with three examples each." Check your prompt has no private details before you send it.
You can now ask an AI assistant money questions safely and know what to check elsewhere.

check.q: What is the safest way to tell an AI about your car payment?
options: Upload a photo of your bank statement
Type your card number so it can check
check.why: A rounded number gives the AI what it needs without any private details.

check.q: The AI explains a money rule and gives a rate. What do you do?
options: Check the rule and rate with an official source
check.why: AI can explain, but rules and rates must be checked with an official source.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a civilian monthly budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a monthly budget table with an AI assistant using rounded numbers.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own rounded numbers, you will build a monthly civilian budget table with an AI assistant, including a line for a cost that changes after service, with totals you checked yourself on a calculator.
In uniform, some costs may have been covered or paid as allowances, such as housing and food allowances, and health care through TRICARE. When you leave service, many of these change or stop. Your civilian budget must cover them from your pay or benefits. Check your own final pay and benefits with your finance office, DFAS or the VA rather than guessing.
Start with four groups: income (pay, benefits), needs (rent, utilities, food, transport, insurance, health), wants (eating out, subscriptions), and savings and debt payments. Ask the AI to build the table and add up each group.
Example prompt: "Make a monthly budget table. Income about $3,800. Rent $1,200, utilities $200, groceries $450, car payment $350, gas $160, phone $70, insurance $150, eating out $200, subscriptions $40. Show totals and what is left."
Step by step:
- List your monthly income with rounded numbers.
- List needs, wants, savings and debt payments.
- Ask the AI to build a table with totals and what is left.
- Add any costs that were covered in service and now are not.
- Check the math yourself with a calculator.
Words to know:
- Allowance: money paid in service for a cost like housing or food.
- Need: a cost you must pay to live and work, like rent.
- Want: a cost you can cut, like eating out.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to build your monthly budget table with rounded numbers. Add one line for a cost that was covered while you served. Check the totals with a calculator.
You can now build a monthly civilian budget table with rounded numbers and check its totals.

check.q: What is the difference between a need and a want in a budget?
options: A need is something you must pay, like rent; a want is something you could cut
A need is anything you like
A want is always more expensive
check.why: Needs are must-pay costs; wants are choices you can reduce if money is tight.

check.q: The AI's budget table says your total is $2,950, but the lines look like more. What do you do?
options: Add the lines yourself on a calculator and fix the total
check.why: AI can make math mistakes, so you check totals yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Spotting money scams aimed at veterans
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot the warning signs of a money scam and know what to do.
This lesson builds toward: Given a message or offer about money or benefits, you will identify the warning signs of a scam and choose a safe response, paying nothing and sharing no codes or private details.
Scammers target veterans because of benefits and pensions. Common traps include offers to "buy" your future pension or benefit payments for a lump sum now (pension advances), people charging to file VA claims or "increase" your rating, fake job offers, and calls pretending to be the VA.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau warns service members and veterans about pension advances and explains your money rights. Scammers now use AI too, to write real-looking messages and even copy voices.
Warning signs: they rush you, ask for an upfront fee, ask for gift cards or a wire transfer, or ask for a code sent to your phone. Stop, hang up, and call back on a number you find yourself on va.gov or the official site. You can also paste a suspicious message into an AI and ask "What are the warning signs in this?", after removing your private details.
Step by step:
- Notice pressure, upfront fees, gift cards, wire transfers or code requests.
- Stop and do not pay or share anything.
- Find the official number yourself and call back.
- Remove private details, then ask AI to point out the warning signs.
- Report it if you lost money.
Words to know:
- Pension advance: an offer to pay you a lump sum now in exchange for your future pension or benefit payments, often at a very high cost.
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
Official sources:
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Military financial lifecycle
Try it now: Write a short example of a scam text offering to "increase your VA rating for a fee". Ask an AI assistant to list its warning signs. Then write what you would do if you got it.
You can now spot the warning signs of money scams aimed at veterans and respond safely.

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a scam?
options: A letter you asked the VA to send
Pressure to pay fast, with gift cards or an upfront fee
check.why: Rushing you and asking for gift cards or upfront fees are classic scam signs.

check.q: A text says your benefits will stop unless you send the code you just got. What do you do?
options: Do not reply; contact the VA on a number you find yourself
check.why: Real agencies do not ask for your codes; you contact them using a number you found yourself.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Goals, routine and real help

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Setting money and life goals
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three clear goals with a number and a date, and break one into steps with AI.
This lesson builds toward: For money and life after service, you will write three goals with a number and a date and break one into weekly steps with AI, with every goal measurable and dated.
A goal works when it is specific, measurable and has a date: "Save $1,000 for emergencies by 31 March" beats "save more". The same is true for life goals: "finish my certification course by June" or "run three times a week".
Write three goals: one money goal, one career or learning goal, and one health or family goal. Then ask an AI to break one into weekly steps: "Break this goal into weekly steps: save $1,000 by 31 March. I can cut about $60 a week from eating out and subscriptions."
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has free tools for service members, including a goal-setting worksheet. Use it with your AI plan.
Step by step:
- Write one money goal, one career goal and one health or family goal.
- Give each a number and a date.
- Ask AI to break one goal into weekly steps.
- Put the first step on your calendar.
Words to know:
- Emergency fund: money saved for surprise costs like a car repair.
- Measurable: you can count it, so you know when it is done.
Official sources:
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Military financial lifecycle (goal-setting worksheet)
Try it now: Write your three goals with a number and a date. Ask an AI assistant to break your money goal into weekly steps.
You can now write clear goals and break one into weekly steps with AI help.

options: It has a number and a date
check.why: A number and a date let you see whether you met the goal.

check.q: You want to save $600 in 3 months. What do you give the AI to break it into steps?
options: The goal, the date and what you can realistically put toward it
check.why: The goal, date and a realistic amount let the AI make useful weekly steps.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Building a weekly routine
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a weekly routine with three goal blocks using an AI assistant.
This lesson builds toward: Using your goals, you will build a weekly routine with three goal blocks, including a weekly budget review, and review and adjust it each week.
Military life ran on a schedule. Civilian life often does not, and many veterans say losing that structure is one of the hardest parts of transition. You can build your own.
Give the AI your fixed times and your goals: "I work 8 to 5 Monday to Friday. My goals: study for my certification 4 hours a week, exercise 3 times a week, review my budget once a week. Make a simple weekly schedule as a table."
Keep it realistic. Leave free time and family time. Review the routine each Sunday and adjust it; a plan is a plan until the first contact, and you adapt.
Step by step:
- List your fixed times: work, school, family.
- List your three goals from Lesson 4.
- Ask AI for a weekly schedule table.
- Add free time and family time.
- Review and adjust it each week.
Words to know:
- Routine: things you do at regular times each week.
- Time block: a set time on your calendar for one task.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to make your weekly schedule with three goal blocks, including one weekly budget review. Put it on your phone calendar or print it.
You can now build a realistic weekly routine that makes time for your goals.

check.q: What is a goal block in a weekly routine?
options: A reminder to pay a scammer
A list of every task you ever did
A set time each week to work on one goal
check.why: A goal block is time you set aside on a regular day to move a goal forward.

check.q: You skipped two goal blocks this week because of appointments. What do you do?
options: Review the routine and move the blocks to times that work
check.why: A routine works when you review it each week and adjust it to real life.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting free, official money help
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the right official source for a money question and write the question down.
This lesson builds toward: Given a money question, you will choose the right official source or counselor and write the question down, checking AI money answers before acting on them.
Some money questions need a person or an official answer: VA benefits and pay, debts, taxes, credit problems, retirement choices, or anything legal. AI can help you write the question clearly, but it should not be the final answer.
Free official help includes: the VA (va.gov) for VA benefits and payments; Military OneSource, which offers free financial counseling to service members and eligible family members (check its eligibility guide to see whether you still qualify after separation); and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (consumerfinance.gov) for your money rights and complaints.
Investments and retirement accounts are personal decisions. This course does not recommend any. Talk to a qualified, trustworthy professional, and be careful with anyone who promises big, fast returns.
Step by step:
- Write your money question in one or two sentences.
- Ask AI to help make it clear, with no private details.
- Choose the right source: VA, Military OneSource or CFPB.
- Contact them using the number or site you found yourself.
Words to know:
- Financial counseling: free or low-cost help from a trained counselor to plan and fix money problems.
- CFPB: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: the U.S. agency that protects people in money matters.
Official sources:
- Military OneSource: Financial counseling
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Military financial lifecycle
- VA: Careers and employment (VA benefits and counseling)
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page plan: your monthly budget from Lesson 2 with a pay-change line, your weekly routine with three goal blocks, and one money question with the official source you will take it to. Check it has no account numbers or private details.
You can now choose the right free official source for a money question and bring a clear question to it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Monthly budget Income, needs, wants, savings or debt payments are missing, or the totals are wrong. All five parts are there with rounded numbers, and the totals were checked on a calculator. The learner can say which want they would cut first if money gets tight. Pay-change line No line for a cost or pay that changes after service. One line shows a cost that was covered in service or a pay change after service. The learner notes where they confirmed their final pay or benefits. Weekly routine The routine has fewer than three goal blocks or no budget review. Three goal blocks, including a weekly budget review, plus free and family time. The routine is on a phone calendar or printed, with a set day to review it. No private details The plan or a prompt includes an account, card or identity number. No account numbers or private details anywhere. The learner can show the rounded prompts they used. Question for an official source No money question, or no source named. One clear money question and the right official source or counselor for it. The learner has booked or contacted that source. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why write down your money question before you contact an official source?
options: So you can post it online
So you ask the right place clearly and get a useful answer
So the AI can answer it instead
So you never need to ask
check.why: A clear written question helps the counselor or agency give you the right answer.

check.q: You have a question about your VA payments. Where do you take it?
check.why: Questions about VA payments go to the VA itself.
